evidence.title: Vibe Coding to Democratize Dementia mHealth Development: Preliminary Findings
evidence.venue: Studies in health technology and informatics
evidence.outcome: Presence of data encryption in vibe-coded dementia mHealth prototypes
evidence.effect: None of the three prototypes implemented data encryption; absence of security measures in all prototypes.
evidence.quote: Notably, no group implemented user authentication or data encryption.

commentary.bottom_line: Thirty-four sources endorse encrypting patient data used by AI at rest and in transit, but no study tests whether this practice reduces interception or exposure of patient data in AI systems. The only supplied study documents the hazard, finding no encryption in any of three student-built dementia app prototypes.

perspectives.view: No supplied study compares AI deployments with and without encryption on any outcome, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single hazard study is a level 4 offline assessment of three student prototypes. It shows that encryption can be omitted in practice, but it does not measure whether adding encryption prevents exposure.

None of three vibe-coded dementia mHealth prototypes implemented data encryption, which suggests that rapidly built AI tools may reach users without basic data protection. Encryption would address one failure mode, interception of stored or transmitted data, but the supplied evidence does not show how often exposure occurs in deployed clinical AI or how much encryption reduces it.

The endorsements tie encryption to existing HIPAA security practice, and the FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software asks manufacturers to address dataset security under its cybersecurity section. Several frameworks use mandatory language. These sources establish an expectation that regulators and assessors may apply, although none reports data on compliance or effect.

commentary.research_gap: No study measures whether encrypting AI training data, inference logs, backups, and vendor API channels reduces breaches or unauthorized access compared with partial or absent encryption. Studies are needed that audit encryption coverage across deployed clinical AI systems and vendor integrations and that link coverage to breach incidents, along with estimates of implementation cost and performance effects on inference.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and the one hazard study did not report participant populations, so no evidence addresses Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups. Safety-net organizations with smaller security budgets may face greater difficulty verifying encryption across vendor channels, but the supplied evidence cannot confirm or quantify that risk.
